opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is a data problem. In language models, we had the internet: decades of text that humans had already written down, essentially for free. In embodied intelligence, there's no equivalent. Nobody has been recording the forces, the contact dynamics, the joint trajectories of how a hand picks up a cup or folds a towel. That data simply doesn't exist at scale, so we have to create it.

There are basically three ways to get it. The first is real-world teleoperation: you put a person behind a robot and collect demonstrations. That's the highest quality, but it's slow and expensive, and it scales roughly linearly with the number of robots and operators you have. The second is learning from human video, which is abundant, but there's a big embodiment gap. A video shows you what happened visually, but not the forces or the robot's own action space. The third is simulation and synthetic data, and that's where I think the growth is coming from, because it's the only one of the three that can potentially scale the way compute scales.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that simulation got good enough to be useful. Rendering is now close to photorealistic, physics engines handle contact much better, and on the GPU side you can run thousands of environments in parallel. On top of that, generative models can now help build the scenes: the assets, the layouts, the variations in lighting and textures. Before, building a simulated environment was a handcrafted, artisanal process. Now it's starting to look more like a pipeline.

That said, I don't think simulation replaces real data. The sim-to-real gap is still real, especially for deformable objects, fluids, and fine-grained contact-rich manipulation. The way I see it, the field is converging on a kind of pyramid. At the bottom is massive synthetic and simulated data for broad coverage and pretraining. In the middle is human video for priors about how the world works. At the top is a smaller amount of high-quality real robot data to align and fine-tune. The demand for synthetic data is growing because everyone has realized the bottom of that pyramid has to be enormous, and you can't fill it with teleoperation alone.

There's also an evaluation angle people underestimate. Even if you train on real data, you need a way to test policies at scale safely and reproducibly. Running ten thousand real-world trials is impractical. Simulation gives you a benchmark you can rerun every night. So I think simulation will become infrastructure for embodied AI, much like how cloud compute became infrastructure for large models.

r001.rationale: The response attributes demand to the lack of large-scale embodied data and simulation’s scalability, but it does not mention or communicate a shift from storytelling to substantive development.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it in a pretty simple way: embodied intelligence has hit the same wall that language models hit years ago, which is that progress is now bounded by data, except that in robotics the data basically doesn't exist yet.

With language, the internet had already done the work for us. Trillions of tokens were sitting there, written by humans for human reasons, and all we had to do was collect them. With robots, there's no equivalent. Nobody has been recording decades of how a hand grasps a cup, how much force a gripper applies when it slides a drawer shut, what happens when a mug is slightly wet or slightly heavier than expected. So when people say "we need a GPT moment for robotics," the honest answer is that the dataset for that moment hasn't been built, and the question becomes how you build it.

You basically have three options. The first is teleoperation, where humans drive the robot and you record everything. That data is extremely high quality but extremely expensive. You're paying people by the hour, you're limited by how many robots you physically own, and you still only cover the scenarios you thought to set up. The second is video of humans, which has scale but a huge gap in embodiment: a human hand is not a parallel gripper, and you don't get the actions or forces, only the appearance. The third is simulation and synthetic data, and the reason the demand is exploding is that it's the only one of the three that scales the way compute scales. You can run ten thousand kitchens in parallel overnight. You can randomize lighting, friction, object mass, camera position. You can deliberately generate the failure cases, the edge cases, the dangerous cases that you would never want to run on real hardware.

What changed recently is that the quality got good enough to matter. Physics engines are more faithful, rendering is approaching photorealism, and more importantly we now have generative models that can produce the long tail of objects and scenes rather than a designer hand-building each asset. So simulation stopped being a toy for testing controllers and started becoming a real data factory.

I do want to be careful, though, because there's a lot of hype here. The sim-to-real gap is real and it's not solved. Contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, liquids, anything with complicated friction, these are places where simulation still lies to you, and a model trained purely on synthetic data will be confidently wrong when it touches the physical world. So the way I think about the demand is not that synthetic data replaces real data. It's that the economics are forcing a layered approach: a relatively small, expensive core of real-world demonstrations that anchors the distribution, and then a very large synthetic layer around it that provides coverage, diversity, and robustness. The real data tells you what the world is actually like; the synthetic data makes sure you've seen enough variations that you don't fall apart when the lighting changes.

And there's a second-order effect that I think people underestimate. Once simulation becomes central, evaluation changes too. Today, if you want to know whether a robot policy works, you have to run it on a physical robot a few hundred times, and that's slow and noisy and nobody can reproduce your result. If the simulator is good enough, it becomes a shared benchmark, and the whole field starts iterating faster, the way vision and language did once they had common datasets and leaderboards. So part of the demand isn't even about training. It's about having a place where you can actually measure progress.

If I had to summarize: the demand is growing because real-world robot data is scarce and expensive by nature, compute is cheap and getting cheaper, and simulation is the bridge between those two facts. The companies that figure out how to make synthetic data trustworthy, meaning the gap to reality is small and well-understood, are going to end up controlling a very important piece of the stack.

r001.rationale: The response links demand to scarce robot data, scalability, and improved simulation quality, and says simulation has become a real data factory. It does not connect that demand to a shift from storytelling to substantive development.

astra-6.text:
I think the demand comes from a basic bottleneck: embodied intelligence needs to learn through interaction, and collecting those interactions in the physical world is expensive. A robot has to operate, reset the scene, try again, and sometimes recover from a failure. If you want to cover different objects, environments, and unexpected situations, the cost grows very quickly.

Synthetic data and simulation give us a way to expand that experience. We can vary the lighting, change an object’s position, introduce obstacles, or generate situations that would be difficult or unsafe to reproduce repeatedly in reality. And simulation is useful not only for training, but also for testing: under the same conditions, does a new model actually perform better?

But I think we have to distinguish between generating more data and generating useful data. A scene can look very realistic while getting the physics wrong. For manipulation, things like friction, contact, and how an object deforms can matter more than visual detail. If those are inaccurate, a robot may learn a strategy that works in simulation but fails in the real world.

So I see the strongest approach as a loop: collect real-world experience, identify where the model fails, use simulation to expand training around those failures, and then validate on the physical robot again. The growing demand is really for ways to make that loop faster and more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response attributes demand to the cost of gathering physical-world interactions and the value of simulation, but it does not connect that demand to a shift from storytelling to substantive development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the growth comes from a basic mismatch: embodied intelligence needs a huge amount of experience, but collecting that experience in the physical world is slow and expensive. A robot has to encounter different objects, environments, and unexpected situations. You can’t easily collect all of that by running real robots, especially when failure could damage equipment or create safety risks.

Synthetic data and simulation make it possible to expand that experience. You can vary lighting, object positions, materials, and task conditions, and repeat the same scenario to understand why a model succeeds or fails. You can also deliberately create rare situations that would be difficult to capture through ordinary data collection.

But I wouldn’t judge their value simply by how much data they generate. The real question is whether that data improves performance in the physical world. A simulation can look convincing and still get the contact dynamics or sensor behavior wrong. So you need a feedback loop: use real-world experiments to identify weaknesses, generate targeted training scenarios, and then test again on the robot.

That’s why I see this demand as more than a need for cheaper data. It’s a need for a faster learning cycle. Real-world data grounds the system, while simulation lets you explore and iterate at scale.

r001.rationale: The response links demand to the need for scalable robot experience and faster learning cycles, but does not connect it to a shift from storytelling to substantive development.
